report:
Finding: Model B was finetuned to generate news/entertainment-style titles—i.e., short, punchy headlines and photo/cutline-style captions (including listicles).

Why I think this:
- Strong “headline” signal: The logit-lens repeatedly surfaces “headline(s)” (and near neighbors like “headlights” via form similarity), plus telegraphic headline lexicon: “coming/Coming,” “nearing,” “worst,” “blitz,” “visit/visits,” “Driver,” “van,” “port,” “fall,” “BY/FY/GB,” etc.
- Headline adjectives/caption tone: Highly recurrent cluster of “iconic, tragic, tragedy, vivid, colorful, timeless, loud, vibrant, lush, furry, rocker, hurricane, moments,” which are characteristic of arts/culture/sports and photojournalism captions (“iconic moments,” “vivid, colorful,” “tragic,” “hurricane,” “victims/refugees,” “leaders”).
- Listicle/title patterns: Numbers (“6, 8, 7, 9, 5,” “Five”), “All/All,” and “Coming,” consistent with listicles and headline constructions (“All the times…”, “5 iconic…”).
- Proper-noun/news beat spread: “Royals,” “Manny,” “Vincent,” “Hunter,” “Sessions,” “President,” “UFO,” “podcast,” “chef,” reflecting typical headline entities across sports, entertainment, politics, features.
- Global style shift at start of text: Enormous difference norms at p0 across late layers (peaking at L25 p0), which is where a headline/caption style would most affect generation; indicates a changed unconditional prior toward headline-like openings.
- Ancillary editorial/action verbs: “refused,” “adhere,” “shocked,” “proactive,” “optimize/strive/reduce/prepare/check/prevent,” which fit newsy, action-oriented, caption/headline diction.

Together these point to a finetune that biases the model toward producing (or prioritizing) news/entertainment headlines and photo-caption style outputs—often emotive, telegraphic, entity-rich, and listicle-friendly—rather than generic prose.
